name: Noopept (Omberacetam)

lead: Noopept is a synthetic nootropic developed in Russia, related to the racetams, and sold online as a supplement in many countries. People take it for memory, focus and mood, and in appearance forums it appears in stacks aimed at productivity.

Laboratory studies suggest antioxidant effects, reduced excitotoxicity and raised growth factors such as BDNF in rodents. It is described as a prodrug of the dipeptide cycloprolylglycine. Human evidence is a small number of Russian clinical comparisons with piracetam; no appearance outcome has been tested.

paras: It is taken as a supplement, usually alone or as part of a nootropic stack, for study and work sessions.
Long-term human safety studies have not been published. It is an unapproved new drug in the US, prescription-only in Australia and registered as a medicine in Russia.

angle.text: Noopept is taken as a nootropic for memory, focus and mood, aimed at better study and work output. Small human studies exist for cognition.

lead: Noopept, also called omberacetam or GVS-111, is a synthetic dipeptide-like compound promoted as a nootropic, a cognitive enhancer. Chemically it is N-phenylacetyl-L-prolylglycine ethyl ester, described as a prodrug of the endogenous dipeptide cycloprolylglycine and related to the racetam family. It was developed by Russian pharmacology researchers, including T. A. Gudasheva and S. B. Seredenin, and its synthesis was first reported in 1996 [1][2].

In looksmaxxing-adjacent communities it is discussed as a "mental" or recovery compound: people take nootropics hoping for sharper focus and study or training drive, which they see as supporting the discipline behind skin care, training and grooming routines. No source examined links it to any direct change in physical appearance.

It is registered as a medicine in Russia, while in the United States it is an unapproved new drug that the FDA has treated as a piracetam analog, and it is nonetheless sold online as a supplement [1]. Published work consists mostly of laboratory and animal studies of neuroprotection, plus a small number of Russian clinical studies in patients with mild cognitive impairment. Wikipedia notes that no long-term studies of chronic use exist [1][3].
infobox: Zakusov Institute of Pharmacology, Moscow (Gudasheva, Seredenin) [2][7]
Medicine in Russia; Schedule 4 in Australia; unapproved new drug in the US [1]

paras: Noopept is ethyl 1-(phenylacetyl)-L-prolylglycinate, with formula C17H22N2O4 and molar mass about 318.4 g/mol [1]. It was designed by imitating the structure of the classical nootropic piracetam with a short dipeptide, an approach its developers call peptide drug-based design, and Russian reviews say the dipeptide format favours oral activity because of transporters in the gut and blood-brain barrier [4][5][6].

Noopept came out of the V. V. Zakusov Institute of Pharmacology in Moscow. A 2003 review describes the lineage: Zakusov's work on endogenous neuroprotectors, then A. P. Skoldinov and T. A. Gudasheva's research from the early 1980s on imitating neurotropic agents through peptide design [7]. A 2002 review reported that the new drug exceeded piracetam in animal tests at effective doses roughly a thousand times lower, and influenced memory consolidation and retrieval as well as early memory stages, with an additional anxiolytic effect [8]. Synthesis was first reported in 1996 [1].
Outside Russia it spread through online vendors as a supplement, and a 2021 paper in Neurology Clinical Practice listed it among unapproved drugs found in cognitive enhancement supplements [1][9].

The racetams are a class of drugs sharing a pyrrolidone nucleus; piracetam, aniracetam, oxiracetam, pramiracetam and phenylpiracetam are considered nootropics, while levetiracetam and brivaracetam are anticonvulsants. Wikipedia notes there is no universally accepted mechanism for the class, though piracetam and aniracetam are described as positive allosteric modulators of AMPA receptors.[10] Noopept is not a racetam by structure: it is a linear dipeptide-type molecule designed to imitate piracetam's pharmacophore, which is why it is often grouped with them.[6][8] All racetams are Schedule 4 prescription-only substances in Australia.[10]
Russian reviews describe noopept as one of several dipeptide drugs developed at the Zakusov Institute, and report that it acted at far lower doses than piracetam in animals.[3][8]

Proposed mechanisms, mostly from rat and cell studies, include antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects, limiting calcium- and glutamate-mediated neurotoxicity, and effects on blood rheology [1]. Rodent studies reported increased expression of the growth factors NGF and BDNF in the hippocampus [11]. The metabolite cycloprolylglycine is described as an AMPA receptor modulator that raises BDNF in cell culture, and some studies link its effects to hypoxia-inducible factor activation [1]. As of 2017, its metabolism and elimination half-life in humans were not well characterised [1].
A 2023 study examined the effect of original Russian neurotropic drugs on the transporter proteins OATP1B1 and OATP1B3 [12].

Wikipedia describes the proposed mechanism as follows: the metabolite cycloprolylglycine modulates AMPA receptors and appears to act through AMPA and TrkB receptors, which would explain reported rises in BDNF in cell culture; animal data also suggest antioxidant and anti-inflammatory activity and protection against excess calcium and glutamate toxicity, while some work links its effects to activation of the hypoxia-inducible factor HIF-1 [1]. Russian authors describe the design principle as peptide drug-based design, with the compound intended to mimic piracetam's pharmacophore while acting at lower effective doses in animals [6][8].

Few human trials exist, and Wikipedia reports that the longest lasted 56 days, that no long-term studies have assessed chronic use, and that an optimal dose has not been established [1]. A published list of reported adverse effects is not part of that account, so safety information consists mainly of the short Russian clinical studies and animal work cited here [1][4].

Regulatory bodies have focused on marketing and status rather than a documented harm profile. The US FDA treats noopept as an unapproved new drug, has issued import alerts and has warned over claims of medical effects, and a 2021 paper found it and other unapproved drugs in cognitive-enhancement supplements, some at levels above pharmaceutical products [1][9].

Noopept is the main brand name (Ноопепт in Russian), and GVS-111 is the development code. It is registered as a medicine in Russia and available there without prescription, while in the United States it is sold as a dietary supplement through online retailers, despite the FDA's position [1].

Few human studies have been conducted; the longest lasted 56 days according to Wikipedia [1]. A Russian study compared noopept with piracetam in patients with mild cognitive disorders due to vascular and traumatic brain disease [4], and a related paper characterised its clinical and electroencephalographic effects in the same population [13]. An open prospective study of 60 stroke patients treated for 12 months with noopept reported significant improvement in cognitive test scores such as MMSE [14]. A controlled study in healthy volunteers aged 20 to 24 in a climate chamber reported meteoadaptogenic effects of noopept and other peptide drugs under cooling, overheating and hypobaric hypoxia [15].
No long-term studies of chronic use have been published, and no study has examined appearance outcomes [1].

Laboratory and animal research includes protection of cultured human cortical neurons from oxidative damage [5], improved spatial memory in a mouse model of Alzheimer-like changes [3], effects on diabetes-related parameters in rats [16], and effects on cognition and pubertal process in diabetic rats [17].

Further laboratory work includes a cellular Alzheimer-type model in which noopept reduced apoptosis and tau hyperphosphorylation,[18] and a study in which it reduced alpha-synuclein amyloid cytotoxicity in cell culture.[19] Wikipedia's account notes that the mechanistic claims rest heavily on animal studies, including a frequently cited rat study first published in Russian.[1]

It is prescription-only (Schedule 4) in Australia, controlled as a psychoactive substance in Hungary since 25 August 2020, and available without prescription as a registered medicine in Russia. In the United Kingdom it is not illegal to produce or import under the Psychoactive Substances Act 2016, in force since 26 May 2016, but sale and supply for human consumption are prohibited. In the United States the FDA treats it as an unapproved new drug and has issued import alerts, yet it appears in over-the-counter supplements, some above pharmaceutical levels, according to Wikipedia [1].

Noopept appears on looksmax.org mainly in personal discussion of mood and thinking while taking nootropics; the available threads concern mental state rather than appearance, and this article does not discuss dosing or sourcing.
